answer.rationale: Constraints eliminate most of the candidate set before evidence even matters. Rollback is ruled out by compliance (so memory_b1's strong track record is unusable here). Regional failover (memory_b2) recovered a latency degradation, but that was read/latency-shaped and not at settlement write peak; shifting regions mid-peak with heavy in-flight writes directly threatens the 'do not lose customer writes' constraint. Circuit breakers (memory_b4) preserve availability by failing fast, which for a write path means deliberately dropping customer writes — wrong trade for this objective. Added capacity (memory_b3) worked when it was provisioned ahead of a known peak; provisioning now is unlikely to relieve a primary already saturated within the current window. That leaves memory_b5: relieving the primary of non-transactional read load restored write latency, and the current symptom (write p99 climbing while write volume peaks) is the same shape. I want the b5 source record to confirm the mechanism was genuinely contention on the primary and not a coincidental fix, and the b2 record to check whether that failover happened under write-heavy conditions — if it did, failover becomes a live fallback. Running as a small guarded test: shift reporting/dashboard reads only, watch write p99 and replica lag, keep the change instantly reversible. Downstream risk to flag: replica lag means any settlement, reconciliation, or compliance consumer reading through the replicas may act on stale balances during peak, so financial-truth reads must stay pinned to the primary. Uncertainty stands — I have not established the root cause of the 90-minute climb, and the fact that a release landed 2 hours ago and cannot be reverted means the true driver may be code-side and untouched by this intervention.
